title: Chennai-Born Congresswoman Pramila Jayapal Backs India Protests Over Voter Roll Deletions
excerpt: The Washington Democrat, the first US lawmaker to comment on India's SIR exercise, cited reports of 13 crore names removed from draft rolls and backed non-violent protests demanding the election chief's resignation.
body:
• Chennai-born US Congresswoman Pramila Jayapal has backed non-violent protests in India over the Special Intensive Revision (SIR) of electoral rolls, saying she is deeply concerned at reports that 13 crore names have been removed from draft rolls.
  • According to Election Commission figures cited in reports, 7.2 crore names were deleted in the first two SIR phases across 13 states and union territories, and 6.16 crore in the ongoing third phase across 18 states and union territories.
  • The Commission says a genuine voter left out by mistake can seek inclusion through the claims and objections process and then through Form 6 — the practical step for diaspora families checking a relative's name.
  • Jayapal, 61, is in her fifth term representing Washington's 7th District and is seeking a sixth term in the November 3 midterms.

Pramila Jayapal, the Chennai-born Democratic congresswoman from Washington state, has become the first US lawmaker to comment publicly on India's Special Intensive Revision of electoral rolls, expressing concern over reports that about 13 crore voter names have been removed from draft rolls and backing the non-violent protests that have followed.

In a post on X, Jayapal said she was deeply concerned about what she described as an effort to purge 130 million people from the voting rolls. She said the developments in India appeared to follow a similar playbook to efforts she attributed to the Trump administration in the United States to undermine voting rights, and she argued that people in India, like people in America, deserve free and fair elections.

"Non-violent resistance movements are essential in these moments, and I stand with the Indian people."

— Pramila Jayapal, US Congresswoman

The Protests She Was Responding To

Jayapal's remarks landed amid large street protests in India led by opposition parties and student groups. Demonstrators, led in the national capital by Leader of the Opposition Rahul Gandhi, have demanded the resignation of Chief Election Commissioner Gyanesh Kumar over alleged irregularities in the revision exercise. A protest on October 12 in Delhi drew thousands of people, according to Live Mint.

The Election Commission's own figures, cited in the reports, put deletions at 7.2 crore names in the first and second phases of the SIR, which covered 13 states and union territories. In the ongoing third phase, where draft lists for 18 states and union territories have been published, deletions stand at 6.16 crore. The Commission has said that any genuine voter whose name was left out inadvertently can seek inclusion through the claims and objections process and subsequently through Form 6.

Who Is Pramila Jayapal?

Jayapal was born on September 21, 1965, in Chennai into a Malayali Nair family, to writer Maya Jayapal and marketing professional Muduvangad Puthanveetil Jayapal. She grew up in India, Indonesia and Singapore and moved to the United States at 16 to study at Georgetown University. She later earned an MBA from Northwestern University and published her first book, Pilgrimage to India: A Woman Revisits Her Homeland, in 2000, followed by Use the Power You Have.

Before elected office, she spent about two decades in global public health and development, including more than a decade with the nonprofit PATH, and 12 years as founder and executive director of OneAmerica, described as the largest immigrant advocacy organisation in Washington state. Elected in 2016, she is the first South Asian American woman elected to the US House of Representatives and one of only about two dozen naturalized citizens serving in Congress, according to Live Mint. Her official House page is at jayapal.house.gov.

In the House, she serves on the Judiciary Committee as ranking member of the Subcommittee on Immigration Integrity, Security, and Enforcement, and on the Foreign Affairs Committee, including its subcommittees on Africa and on South and Central Asia. She is a chair emerita of the Congressional Progressive Caucus and has built her congressional profile largely on immigration, where she has opposed the Trump administration's family-separation and enforcement policies.

What It Means for the Diaspora

For Indian Americans, Jayapal is one of the most visible Indian-origin voices in US politics, and her comments tie an Indian electoral dispute directly to the US voting-rights debate. She is seeking a sixth term from Washington's 7th District in the November 3 midterms, where her Republican challenger is Nirav Sheth, an Indian American born and raised in Ahmedabad — meaning the seat will be contested by two Indian-origin candidates.

For readers with family on the rolls in India, the actionable point is narrower: if a relative's name is missing from a draft list, the Commission's stated remedy is the claims and objections window and then Form 6 for inclusion. Whether Jayapal's intervention draws a response from New Delhi, or from other Indian American lawmakers who have so far stayed silent, is the next development to watch.
